messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 54-year-old North American forester married to his high school sweetheart, has been struggling with intense feelings of guilt and fear since an accident at work six months ago. While working in the woods, John accidentally caused a chainsaw to cut into his colleague’s leg, resulting in a serious injury that required immediate medical attention. The moment the chainsaw sliced through flesh, the sound of metal against bone still rings in John's ears whenever he experiences physical pain. This somatic trigger has led him to feel unable to relax even when he knows he is safe. He feels like his body remembers the trauma just as vividly as his mind does, replaying the position and movements during the accident whenever he feels bodily discomfort. John’s inability to relax extends beyond his work; at home, he watches his surroundings closely for any sign of danger, especially from strangers approaching him in ordinary situations. His wife notices that he is always on edge when they go out, constantly scanning their environment as if expecting something terrible to happen again. John believes that watching others carefully might help him prevent another incident. Whenever the memories come back, John feels his body reenacting the movements and positions from the accident, intensifying his feelings of rage and grief. The memory of his colleague’s pain brings overwhelming grief, while the thought of how he could have prevented it leads to intense anger directed at himself. These memories are so vivid that they often trigger physical sensations in John's own body, making him feel as though he is reliving the moment. John has come to believe that there must be something inherently wrong with him—that his intrinsic fault led to this accident. This belief exacerbates his feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt. He can't rely on himself anymore and feels that he is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined him as a forester. John's fear of causing another injury has kept him away from the forest, leading him to avoid tasks that require physical proximity or handling tools. John’s wife has noticed how his fears have affected their relationship and daily life. He avoids going out with her because he is terrified something similar could happen again in public. This avoidance has led to tension at home as they spend less time together outside the house. John's fear of being unable to protect himself or those around him has deepened his sense of incapability. The cycle of triggers and memories continues to tighten its grip on John. Whenever he feels physical pain, it sets off a chain reaction: he remembers the accident, which brings back intense grief and rage, reinforcing his negative beliefs about himself. These beliefs then make it even harder for him to relax or trust in his abilities, making any physical discomfort feel like a potential trigger. What finally brought John to seek help was when his wife confronted him about how their relationship was suffering because he refused to leave the house. She expressed her concern that if things continued this way, they might drift apart. The thought of losing his marriage is what pushed John over the edge; it made him realize that unless he gets help, he risks losing everything that matters to him. John hopes for a return to normalcy and peace of mind, but most of all, he fears falling further into himself and becoming isolated from those who care about him. He knows that without intervention, his life will continue to shrink until there is nothing left but fear and regret.
